On the $4$-billiards table (the unit square with corners $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$), a ball starts at $(0.2,0.6)$ moving towards the point $(0.3,0.9)$. Is its trajectory periodic or degenerate? (Answer ``periodic'' or ``degenerate''.)
answer: degenerate

solutions.title: Follow the path
solutions.body:
The direction is $(0.1,0.3)$, i.e. slope $3$. Moving up from $(0.2,0.6)$ the ball reaches the top edge $y=1$ at $x=0.2+\frac{0.4}{3}=\frac13$. After reflecting its slope is $-3$, so it reaches the bottom edge $y=0$ at $x=\frac13+\frac13=\frac23$. Reflecting again (slope $3$) it reaches $x=1$ exactly when $y=1$, i.e. at the corner $(1,1)$, a pocket.

The trajectory is **degenerate**.

$$\angle C_{i+1}P_iP_j=\frac12\cdot\frac{360\,((j-i)\bmod n)}{n}=\frac{180\,((j-i)\bmod n)}n.\ \blacksquare$$

solutions.title: Unfold into a straight line
solutions.body:
Tile the plane with unit squares by repeatedly reflecting the table over its edges. Then the trajectory becomes a straight line $L$ starting at the initial point (we may assume it is on an edge by following the trajectory to its first hit), with direction vector $(\delta_x,\delta_y)$. The *Golden L* is the billiards table that is the polygon with vertices $(0,0),(\varphi,0),(\varphi,1),(1,1),(1,\varphi),(0,\varphi)$, where $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ is the golden ratio; its pockets are the six corners and the two additional marked points $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ (see the figure: side lengths $1,\ \varphi-1,\ 1,\ \varphi-1$ as marked). Show that any periodic trajectory on the Golden L has either an undefined slope, or a slope of the form $a+b\varphi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. (Hint: rewind and track the horizontal and vertical distances separately.)
answer: All sides are horizontal or vertical, so $|\text{slope}|=V/H$ where $H,V$ are the total horizontal and vertical distances travelled in a period; each is a sum of distances between lines $x\in\{0,1,\varphi\}$ (resp. $y\in\{0,1,\varphi\}$), hence of the form $\alpha+\beta\varphi$ with integers $\alpha,\beta$, and $\mathbb Q(\varphi)$ is a field.

solutions.title: Horizontal and vertical distances
solutions.body:
Every edge of the table is horizontal or vertical, so each reflection only flips the sign of one component of the velocity. Hence the speeds in the $x$ and $y$ directions, $u=|\dot x|$ and $v=|\dot y|$, never change, and the slope of the trajectory is $\pm\frac vu$ (undefined if $u=0$, in which case we are done; if $v=0$ the slope is $0=0+0\varphi$).

So assume $u,v>0$ and let the trajectory be periodic with period $C$. Over one period the ball travels total horizontal distance $H=uC$ and vertical distance $V=vC$, so $\frac vu=\frac VH$.

*Computing $H$.* The horizontal motion reverses only at vertical edges, which lie on the lines $x=0$, $x=1$, $x=\varphi$. Rewind to a time when the ball is on a vertical edge (the motion is periodic and the ball must reach vertical edges, since $u>0$ and the table is bounded). Between two consecutive vertical-edge hits the horizontal distance travelled is the distance between two different lines among $x=0,1,\varphi$, i.e. one of $1,\ \varphi-1,\ \varphi$. Over one period, $H$ is a sum of such distances, so $H=\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi$ with $\alpha_1,\beta_1\in\mathbb Z$ (because $1,\varphi-1,\varphi$ all lie in $\mathbb Z+\mathbb Z\varphi$).

*Computing $V$.* In the same way, the vertical motion reverses only at horizontal edges, which lie on the lines $y=0,1,\varphi$ (the horizontal edges are at heights $0,1$ and $\varphi$), so $V=\alpha_2+\beta_2\varphi$ with $\alpha_2,\beta_2\in\mathbb Z$.

*The quotient.* $H>0$, and $\varphi$ is irrational so $\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi\neq0$; the number $\frac{\alpha_2+\beta_2\varphi}{\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi}$ lies in the field $\mathbb Q(\varphi)=\{a+b\varphi: a,b\in\mathbb Q\}$ (use $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ and multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $\alpha_1+\beta_1\bar\varphi$ with $\bar\varphi=1-\varphi$; the product $\alpha_1^2+\alpha_1\beta_1-\beta_1^2$ is a nonzero integer). Hence the slope $\pm\frac VH$ is of the form $a+b\varphi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: The orthic triangle (Fagnano)
solutions.body:
Let the triangle be $DEF$ (all angles $<90^\circ$), with $X\in EF$, $Y\in FD$, $Z\in DE$.

**A period-$3$ trajectory is an inscribed triangle with the law of reflection.** After a reflection off an edge the ball moves away from the line of that edge, so it cannot hit the same edge twice in a row. With three hits per period, cyclically, the three hit points $X,Y,Z$ are therefore on three different edges: say $X\in EF$, $Y\in FD$, $Z\in DE$, traversed $X\to Y\to Z\to X$ (or the opposite way). The reflection law at $X$ says that the edge line $EF$ is the external bisector of $\angle YXZ$, and likewise $FD$ at $Y$, $DE$ at $Z$.

**It must be the orthic triangle.** Let $I$ be the incenter of $XYZ$ and let its angles be $x,y,z$. Since an internal bisector is perpendicular to the external bisector, $IX\perp EF$, $IY\perp FD$, $IZ\perp DE$. Then $\angle DZI=\angle DYI=90^\circ$, so $D,Z,I,Y$ lie on the circle with diameter $DI$. Hence $\angle ZDI=\angle ZYI=\frac y2$ (inscribed angles on the chord $ZI$).

On the other hand, the angles at $D$: from the law of reflection, $\angle DZY=\angle EZX=90^\circ-\frac z2$ and $\angle DYZ=\angle FYX=90^\circ-\frac y2$ (the equal angles on either side of the edge), so in triangle $DYZ$ we get $\angle D=\frac{y+z}2=90^\circ-\frac x2$; similarly $\angle E=90^\circ-\frac y2$, $\angle F=90^\circ-\frac z2$. The altitude from $D$ makes an angle $90^\circ-\angle E=\frac y2$ with $DE$, and so does the ray $DI$ (as $\angle ZDI=\frac y2$, with $Z$ on $DE$), and both lie inside angle $D$; so $DI$ is the altitude from $D$. Since $IX\perp EF$ as well, $X$ is the foot of the altitude from $D$. Likewise $Y$ and $Z$ are the feet of the altitudes from $E$ and $F$. So the inscribed triangle is the orthic triangle, which is unique; the two directions of traversal give the two trajectories.

**The orthic triangle works.** As $DEF$ is acute the three feet lie in the interiors of the sides (so none is a pocket). Let $X,Y,Z$ be the feet of the altitudes from $D,E,F$. Since $\angle DZF=\angle DXF=90^\circ$, the points $D,Z,X,F$ lie on a circle with diameter $DF$, so $\angle EXZ=\angle ZDF=\angle D$. Since $\angle DYE=\angle DXE=90^\circ$, the points $D,Y,X,E$ lie on a circle with diameter $DE$, so $\angle FXY=\angle YDE=\angle D$. Hence $XZ$ and $XY$ make equal angles with $EF$: the law of reflection holds at $X$, and by symmetry at $Y$ and $Z$. The path $X\to Y\to Z\to X$ is a periodic trajectory with $3$ hits per period (its three hits are on three different edges, so its combinatorial period is $3$), and its time reverse is the other one.

So there are exactly two. $\blacksquare$

**Setup.** A *billiards table* is a bounded polygon whose corners are *pockets*. A *trajectory* is the path of a ball moving at unit speed along a straight line, reflecting off the edges by the law of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) and stopping if it reaches a pocket. A trajectory $P(t)$ is *degenerate* if $P(t)$ is a pocket for some $t>0$, and *periodic* if there is a constant $C>0$ with $P(t+C)=P(t)$ for all $t$ (the clock may also be run backwards, so $P(t)$ is defined for $t<0$ too); the smallest such $C$ is the *period*. The *combinatorial period* of a periodic trajectory is the number of times it hits an edge during one period (the same edge, or even the same point, may be hit several times and each hit is counted).

A *simple billiards table* is a convex polygon with pockets at its corners. You may use the following theorem.

**Theorem.** For any simple billiards table, if a line segment starts at a point $P_1$ on an edge $e_1$ and ends at a point $P_2$ on an edge $e_2$, with $P_1,P_2$ not pockets, then there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $\overline{P_1P_2}$ is translated perpendicular to its direction by any $t<\epsilon$ and extended/cropped to a segment $\overline{P_1^tP_2^t}$ with $P_1^t$ on $e_1$ and $P_2^t$ on $e_2$, the line $\overline{P_1^tP_2^t}$ does not contain a pocket.

Show that for any periodic trajectory with odd combinatorial period $p$ on a simple billiards table, there exists a periodic trajectory with combinatorial period $2p$.
answer: Unfold the trajectory: after $p$ (odd) reflections the table copy is flipped, after $2p$ it is a translate of the original. A slightly shifted parallel line closes up after $2p$ hits but not after $p$.

solutions.title: Unfold and shift slightly
solutions.body:
Let $T$ be the periodic trajectory with odd combinatorial period $p$, with consecutive hits $T_0,T_1,\dots,T_p=T_0$ on edges $e_0,\dots,e_{p-1},e_p=e_0$.

**Unfolding.** Unfold the table along $T$: reflect the table across each edge hit in turn, so that the trajectory becomes a straight line $L$ crossing copies $\Pi_0,\Pi_1,\Pi_2,\dots$ of the table, where $\Pi_{i+1}$ is the reflection of $\Pi_i$ across the copy of $e_i$ it contains. Let $g_i$ be the isometry carrying $\Pi_0$ to $\Pi_i$; it is a product of $i$ reflections. After $p$ reflections ($p$ odd) the copy $\Pi_p$ is a mirror image of $\Pi_0$ with reversed orientation: $g_p$ is an orientation-reversing isometry mapping $T_0$ to $T_p$ (the point of $L$ where $T$ returns to its start), and mapping $L$ onto itself preserving its direction, so $g_p$ is a glide reflection with axis $L$. After $2p$ reflections $g_{2p}=g_p^2$ is a translation along $L$.

**A nearby trajectory.** The line $L$ is cut into $2p$ consecutive segments $Q_iQ_{i+1}$ ($i=0,\dots,2p-1$), each lying in a copy of the table between two edges, with endpoints that are not pockets (the original trajectory is non-degenerate). Apply the theorem to each segment (folded back into the table): there is $\epsilon_i$ such that any parallel shift by $t<\epsilon_i$ stays away from pockets. Let $\epsilon=\min\epsilon_i$ and fix $0<t<\epsilon$. Let $L_t$ be the line parallel to $L$ at distance $t$ (on one chosen side). The trajectory $R$ whose unfolding is $L_t$ crosses the same copies in the same order, hits the same edges $e_0,\dots,e_{p-1},e_0,\dots$ as $T$ and is non-degenerate.

**Period.** The translation $g_{2p}$ maps $L_t$ to itself, so after $2p$ hits $R$ is back in its initial state: $R$ is periodic and its combinatorial period $d$ divides $2p$. Also $g_i$ depends only on the first $i$ edges hit, which for $R$ are the same as for $T$; if the sequence of hit edges has period $m$ then $g_{km}=g_m^{\,k}$.

- *$d$ odd.* Then $d\mid p$ and the edge sequence has period $d$, so $g_p=g_d^{\,p/d}$. Since $R$ returns to its state after $d$ hits, $g_d$ maps $L_t$ to itself reversing orientation, so it is a glide reflection with axis $L_t$, and so is its odd power $g_p$. But $g_p$ is a glide reflection with axis $L\ne L_t$, a contradiction.
- *$d$ even.* Write $d=2d'$ with $d'\mid p$. The edge sequence of $R$ (which equals that of $T$) has periods $2d'$ and $p$, hence period $\gcd(2d',p)=d'$, which is odd. Then $g_p=g_{d'}^{\,p/d'}$ is an odd power of the orientation-reversing isometry $g_{d'}$, and it is a glide reflection with axis $L$; this forces $g_{d'}$ to be a glide reflection with the same axis $L$. So $g_{d'}$ maps $L$ to itself and carries the initial state of $T$ to its state after $d'$ hits: $T$ returns to its initial state after $d'$ hits. As $p$ is the combinatorial period of $T$, $d'=p$ and $d=2p$.

Hence $R$ is periodic with combinatorial period exactly $2p$. $\blacksquare$
